KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Motion for Recusal                             Page 1 of 11
                 KEVIN KENNEDY’S VERIFIED MOTION FOR RECUSAL
                       OF CHAIRMAN THOMAS J. GLEESON


                                     I.   INTRODUCTION

      Pro se intervenor Kevin Kennedy brings this motion under 16 TAC § 22.3(f)(1) and (g)

and asks for Chairman Thomas J. Gleeson to recuse himself from deliberating or voting on

whether to approve or deny the applications to amend the Certificates of Convenience and

Necessity (CCNs) in Docket Nos. 59182 and 59475, as well as any other deliberations and/or

decisions regarding those dockets and CCN applications.

      Section 22.3(f)(1) requires recusal when a commissioner’s “impartiality has been

reasonably questioned.” The rule’s purpose is to protect each party’s right to a fair and impartial

decision and to maintain the public’s confidence that the Commission will decide a CCN

application on the evidence presented by the parties, without bias. The rule expressly requires

recusal from deciding a particular issue if a party reasonably questions impartiality.

       The Chairman is listed as a confirmed stakeholder at a meeting whose subject, timing,

and list of attendees easily cause a reasonable person to question why Chairman Gleeson would

attend such a meeting. As a result, Chairman Gleeson’s impartiality is hereby reasonably brought

into question and Mr. Kennedy moves for his recusal from 59182 and 59475.




                               II.   THIS MOTION IS TIMELY

      On Saturday, November 14, 2026, Mr. Kennedy first saw and reviewed the Governor’s

Chief of Staff, Robert Black’s calendar and confirmed stakeholder list filed that same day in

Docket No. 59475 as Item 6671. The stakeholder list shows the meeting title, date, and time. It

has checkmarks beside the confirmed names of Chairman Gleeson, as well as representatives


KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Motion for Recusal                                           Page 2 of 11
 from Oncor, AEP, CenterPoint, ERCOT, Amazon, Google, META, Nvidia, and the Governor’s

staff, among others. Mr. Kennedy’s November 14, 2026, review of the stakeholder list sets the

date of his personal knowledge impetus that is the basis for this motion.

       Under § 22.3(g)(1)–(2), the motion must precede the Commission’s scheduled date to

consider the matter, which it timely does here, and must meet the later of two deadlines: ten

working days after the facts became known or 15 days after the proceeding began. The

November 20 filing date of this motion is less than 10 working days after November 14, when

the facts became known to Mr. Kennedy.

       Mr. Kennedy moves before the Commission’s final consideration of the applications,

submits this motion no more than ten working days after the facts became known to him, and he

verifies the facts within his personal knowledge by the attached affidavit. The motion is

complete and timely.

       To deny this motion on any claimed procedural technicality or shortcoming and to not

respond directly and publicly to the reasonableness of the questioning of impartiality, would

undermine the very Commission integrity that 16 TAC § 22.3(f)(1) is intended to secure.




      III.    ONCOR WAS DEVELOPING BOTH SEGMENTS OF IMPORT PATH 2

AND OTHER PERMIAN IMPORT PATHS WHEN THE ROUNDTABLE TOOK PLACE

April 24, 2025. The Commission approved the three 765-kV import paths in ERCOT’s Permian

Basin Reliability Plan. Import Path 2 runs from Bell County East through Big Hill to Sand Lake.

Oncor and LCRA TSC are joint applicants developing the two connecting Import 2 segments. 1



1
 PUC Project No. 55718, Second Order Approving the Reliability Plan for the Permian Basin Region (Apr. 24,
2025). See also Docket No. 57441, Item 54 (Aug. 11, 2025), identifying both segments as Oncor-assigned projects.

line (59029).4

(59029).5

December 16, 2025. Governor’s Office Chief of Staff Robert Black’s calendar set a

“Transmission Roundtable” for 3:30 to 4:30 p.m. The confirmed-stakeholder list marked

Chairman Gleeson, ERCOT CEO Pablo Vegas, and Oncor’s Liz Jones. It also marks

representatives of AEP Texas, CenterPoint, Amazon Web Services, Google, Meta, Nvidia, and

OpenAI. POLITICO described a closed-door meeting about building out the grid and removing

obstacles. It also reported that Oncor confirmed its vice president of regulatory affairs attended. 6

KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Motion for Recusal                                                    Page 4 of 11
 After the roundtable. On December 30, just 14 days later, Oncor requested the docket number

for Big Hill–Sand Lake. On January 15, 2026, 30 days after the meeting, the applicants filed the

59182 CCN application. On March 6, Oncor requested the docket number for Bell County East–

Big Hill. On March 26, 2026, the applicants filed their 59475 CCN application.

              IV.    THE FACTS REASONABLY CALL THE CHAIRMAN’S

                             IMPARTIALITY INTO QUESTION

      At the time of the roundtable, Oncor and LCRA TSC had spent almost one year

developing routes. Six months prior to the meeting, they held public meetings, for both halves of

Import Path 2, to present their preliminary routes. Oncor had originally told landowners it

expected to file the 59475 application in December 2025, the very month of the roundtable. The

application for the 59182 segment was only 30 days from filing. The meeting fell squarely in the

middle of Oncor and LCRA TSC’s overall efforts toward application and approval for both

projects; hardly an appropriate phase of project development for the PUC Chairman to attend

such a meeting.

      The five 765-kV transmission line projects of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP),

spanning over 1,200 miles, would be the first 765-kV lines in Texas and the first segments of a

colossal, 4,000-mile to 5,000-mile bulk 765-kV STEP transmission proposal submitted by

ERCOT and transmission companies, covering virtually the entire State of Texas. The 765-kV

lines are purported to be necessary due in large part to the explosion of data center proposals.

      The meeting subject was transmission. The confirmed stakeholders included Chairman

Gleeson, who would decide the CCN applications, and Oncor, who was preparing to file the

CCN applications. Also listed were representatives from AEP, CenterPoint, ERCOT, Amazon,

Google, META, Nvidia, and the Governor’s staff, among others. These were representatives of



KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Motion for Recusal                                           Page 5 of 11
 many of the largest tech companies in the world who would benefit from the 765-kV lines.

Google had previously advocated directly to the PUC for the 765-kV Permian import lines. 7

       We do not know exactly what was discussed but considering the subject, the persons

involved, the current state of project development, and the timing of the meeting, it would seem

wholly unreasonable to assume the PBRP 765-kV lines, including Import Path 2, would not

likely be key points of discussion at this “Transmission Roundtable”. Additionally, no affected

landowner or representative of the Office of Public Utility Counsel is identified as an attendee on

the list. Lastly, it is not an unreasonable expectation that Chairman Gleeson should and would

decline an invitation to such a meeting, to maintain an appearance of impartiality, but he

apparently did not. Chairman Gleeson’s mere attendance at the meeting raises sufficient doubt,

irrespective of what may or may not have been discussed.

       The question of impartiality bears directly on decisions still to be made. On August 20,

2026, the Administrative Law Judges (ALJs) issued their original Proposal for Decision (PFD),

which recommended denial of the applications. 8 On September 18, Chairman Gleeson signed

the Commission’s order remanding the case back to the ALJs and directed the judges to address

whether the project is needed to meet state or federal reliability standards and what congestion

cost savings consumers could expect. The Commission’s remand asks the ALJs to reconsider

whether these CCN applications should be approved.9 Chairman Gleeson remanded 59182 and

59475 back to the ALJs in spite of the fact that the ALJs’ PFD had already clearly and strongly

recommended denial on the basis of six separate issues, four of which were related to failure to

prove need, which would encompass reliability.



7
  PUC Project No. 55718 - Item 108, Google's Comments on the Siemens PTI Cost-Benefit Analysis of 765kV
Facilities in ERCOT (Apr. 22, 2025)
8
  Docket No. 59475, Proposal for Decision, Item 6578 (Aug. 20, 2026)
9

KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Motion for Recusal                                                  Page 6 of 11
           Many landowners, including Mr. Kennedy, questioned why the Commission remanded

Issues 11 and 13 when the original PFD appeared to already address those issues. That

questionable decision to remand was the immediate backdrop to disclosure of the closed-door

“Transmission Roundtable”. Additionally, the Commission had also recently reversed the public

notification findings of the ALJs in the Dinosaur to Longshore 765-kV line (59315), where those

ALJs had found that Oncor had failed to follow Commission rules regarding notification of about

1,650 landowners. The Commission had cited cases as precedence that affected only a relative

handful of property owners, which seemed far from comparable to the 1,650 disenfranchised

landowners on 59315. 10 Many landowners, including Mr. Kennedy question the Commission

decision. This too was part of the growing backdrop of doubt when the Chairman’s inclusion on

the confirmed stakeholder list for the “Transmission Roundtable” was made public.

          It should not be difficult to acknowledge that the culmination of all these circumstances

gives Mr. Kennedy rational grounds to question the Chairman’s impartiality. Other landowners,

in this and other ongoing 765-kV transmission dockets, have also asserted a similar reasonable

questioning of impartiality and some have made motions for recusal. Visit the Facebook page

STOP: Bell County East – Big Hill 765kv 11 and you will quickly find Mr. Kennedy is far from

alone in his concerns regarding impartiality. To attempt to judge or claim so many as

unreasonable would in itself be unreasonable.

          The “court of public opinion” is not an actual court of law but a metaphorical or figurative

space where society collectively judges actions, controversies, or individuals. The findings of the

court of public opinion is the bar established for recusal by the Commission in their own rule 16

TAC § 22.3(f)(1) that states a commissioner must recuse himself when “the commissioner’s


10
     Docket No. 59315, ALJs’ response to exceptions, Item 5788, pp. 3-4 (Aug. 14, 2026)
11
     https://www.facebook.com/groups/stopbellcountyeastbighill765kv/

KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Motion for Recusal                                                Page 7 of 11
 impartiality has been reasonably questioned”. The Commission recognizes that public

perception and trust in our State officials is paramount. The decisions of the commissioners,

particularly the Chairman, must be above reproach and not subject to reasonable questioning

regarding fairness and impartiality. As required by 16 TAC § 22.3(f)(1), a commissioner must

recuse himself if the commissioner’s impartiality has been reasonably questioned.

       The remaining commissioners should be completely capable of thoughtful consideration

and rendering a proper decision. The Chairman must err on the side of caution. To ignore the

calls for recusal would only serve to feed the fires of distrust and further undermine the integrity

of the State and the Commission. To grant recusal would restore some faith in the honor of the

agency.

       The 59315 ALJs provide further guidance on this matter when in their PFD they cite

PUCT v. City of Denton, No. 15-25-00018, 2026 WL 1595348, at *6 (15th Ct. App. June 4,

2026). The 15th Court of Appeals recently reaffirmed “a state agency has no authority to fail to

follow its own rules; when it does, its acts are arbitrary and capricious.” 12 That 15th Court of

Appeals’ decision applies here; the Chairman is bound to follow his own rules, otherwise, what

is the purpose of having rules. His impartiality is reasonably questioned.




       The correct response is as obvious as it will be impactful.




12
  Docket No. 59315, SOAH Proposal for Decision at 26 & n.89, Item 5719 (July 24, 2026) (“a state agency has no
authority to fail to follow its own rules; when it does, its acts are arbitrary and capricious”).

KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Motion for Recusal                                                     Page 8 of 11
                                          V.    PRAYER

      Mr. Kennedy hereby rightfully and reasonably questions Chairman Gleeson’s impartiality.

The certainty of impartiality is owed to the affected landowner and rate payer parties due to the

enormity of the decision’s consequences. Recusal is the only reasonable option to uphold the

integrity of the Commission, as required by 16 TAC § 22.3(f)(1).

      Mr. Kennedy respectfully requests that Chairman Gleeson grant this motion, issue his

decision within the time limit required by § 22.3(g)(4), and recuse himself from deliberating or

voting on whether to approve or deny the CCN applications in Docket Nos. 59182 and 59475, as

well as any further deliberations and/or decisions regarding 59182 and/or 59475.
